title: SPONSORED: Growing pains: how distributed AI training changes the network between datacenters
gist: A Cisco-sponsored piece argues that synchronous AI training across datacenters ('scale-across') needs far more bandwidth (about 14x conventional DCI), many more coherent optical ports, and deep-buffer routing silicon than traditional DCI, and pitches the Silicon One P200 as the answer. Cisco itself says deployments are early and will take a few years.

insights.claim: Large-scale AI training has already spread beyond single datacenters: Google trained Gemini synchronously across multi-location clusters, Microsoft linked Wisconsin and Georgia AI datacenters, AWS connected clusters for Anthropic, and CoreWeave and Google Cloud announced cross-cloud training.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capex is increasingly about inter-site fabric, not just single-campus build-outs.

insights.claim: Single campuses are strained by compute and power demand; Epoch AI researchers say the largest frontier training runs could draw 4-16GW by 2030, so distributing compute lets operators build where power and space are available.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Power scarcity pushes training toward geographically distributed sites, favoring interconnect vendors.

themes.theme: Why synchronization makes the network a bottleneck

insights.claim: Synchronous training repeats compute and synchronization, so thousands of accelerators exchange gradients at the same moment, producing bursty traffic and incast; a network delay becomes compute delay.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Idle GPUs are the cost of a slow network, so network performance maps directly to training economics.
insights.quote: "If you look at any training job, it is basically a repetition of compute and synchronization,"

insights.claim: Delayed or dropped flows can force retransmission and leave accelerators waiting, and more serious failures can require training to return to a saved checkpoint.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Reliability of inter-site links affects training progress, not only throughput.

insights.claim: Traditional DCI is built for redundancy, reach and asynchronous replication traffic, whereas scale-across makes the inter-site network part of one coordinated computation that needs sufficient bandwidth and predictable delivery.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Existing DCI designs and products may not fit AI training, opening a new product category.

insights.claim: Cisco's modelling says aggregate bandwidth for large distributed AI deployments can reach roughly 14x a conventional DCI baseline.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Vendor-modelled figure; implies a large step-up in optical and routing demand.
insights.quote: According to Cisco modelling of large distributed AI deployments, aggregate bandwidth requirements can reach roughly 14x a conventional DCI baseline.

insights.claim: Cisco estimates that connecting two 100 megawatt AI sites could need 12,000 to 32,000 coherent optical ports, versus roughly 1,000 to 2,000 for conventional DCI between comparable facilities.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Port counts of 10x or more are a demand driver for coherent pluggable optics suppliers.

insights.claim: Short-range datacenter optics cannot carry 400-800 Gbps over hundreds of kilometers, so operators need coherent optics with advanced modulation and DSP; coherent pluggables in router ports avoid separate DWDM transponder banks and save space, power and cooling.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Coherent pluggables are the enabling technology for power-constrained AI sites.

insights.claim: On an 800 Gb/sec link spanning 100 kilometers, Cisco calculates about 100 MB of data can be in flight before congestion feedback reaches the sender, which raises the value of deep-buffer silicon over shallow-buffer datacenter switches.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Gives a quantitative basis for Cisco's deep-buffer positioning against shallow-buffer rivals.

insights.claim: Cisco pairs proactive congestion management, exploiting the repetitive and predictable collective communication of AI training, with a single fully shared deep buffer as a safety net for transient congestion and link failures.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Cisco's architectural argument is avoid the queue and also have somewhere to put traffic when a queue forms.

insights.claim: Cisco's scale-across architecture uses the Silicon One P200, a 51.2 Tb/sec programmable deep-buffer routing processor in the Cisco 8223 and N9000 platforms, with 400G and 800G coherent pluggables and Open Transport 3000 or NCS 1014 for optical transport.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: This is the product stack Cisco is selling into AI interconnect.

insights.claim: Cisco claims Open Transport 3000's multi-rail design reduces power per rail by 75 percent and rack space by 80 percent, and that NCS 1014 provides 12.8 Tb/sec from a 1RU line card.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Vendor claims in a sponsored article, not independently verified.

insights.claim: Cisco argues that having silicon, system and optics teams in one company lets requirements like port density, buffering, power and telemetry feed back into chip design, and that P4-programmable silicon lets network functions evolve without chip replacement.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Vertical integration and programmability are the claimed moat versus merchant-silicon systems.

insights.claim: Scale-across has not settled on a single architecture: Cisco splits it into campus, metro and regional deployments, operators vary in distance, topology and workload design, and Cisco's Itamar Gold says early deployments are underway but will take a few years.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Adoption timing is gradual, so revenue ramps for this category are likely multi-year.
insights.quote: "We are seeing early deployments now, but it is a process and I think it will take a few years,"
insights.locator: Designing a network for distributed training

insights.claim: The article is explicitly sponsored by Cisco, so the claims and figures come from Cisco executives and modelling.
insights.speaker: Stewart Baines
insights.so_what: Discount the framing as vendor marketing when weighing the numbers.
